newsitem.title: USA: Capital still finding developing nations - W.Bank.
newsitem.headline: Capital still finding developing nations - W.Bank.

text.p: Capital should continue flowing to developing nations at record levels and with greater focus on long-term investing, reducing the risks of financial market meltdowns, according to a World Bank report released Thursday.

World Bank chief economist Joseph Stiglitz and economic advisor Amar Battacharya, the study's principal author, noted that certain capital controls can help lengthen the duration of foreign investment and that current inflation posed little threat to developing nations.

The study predicted that developing nations would continue to grow roughly twice as fast as industrial countries, while less opaque market conditions and more reliable banking sector regulations will substantially reduce risks to outside investors.

"With continuing policy reforms, developing countries are expected to offer investors higher risk-adjusted rates of returns and increased opportunities for portfolio diversificiation, suggesting that net flows to developing countries are likely to be sustained in the medium-term," said Battacharya at a briefing.
Having built their financial reserves and worked to limit their trade imbalances, most developing nations should be able to avoid the kind of market panic that shook Mexico in late 1994, he added.
"Markets became more discerning and ... countries became wiser in the wake of that (Mexico) crisis," he said.

While capital controls should not be used in place of sound macroeconomic policies, restrictions on inflows can help encourage investors to be more patient with bets in developing nations, the study found.
"It may be wise to curb lending booms associated with capital inflows by using macroeconomic policies as well as more targeted interventions on the banking sector," Battacharya said.
Stiglitz also cited World Bank research showing that inflation in developing countries remains much lower than that of the 1980s and little or no threat to most emerging market economies.
"The kinds of high levels of inflation that characterized the world in earlier decades has not been seen," said Stiglitz.

"There is relatively little negative effect of moderate levels of inflation below 10 percent or within 15 percent, so that in terms of adverse economic effects from these slight increases in inflation (the risks) are not very significant," he added.
